2027-01-17.title: Second Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: Speak, for your servant is listening
Here am I, Lord; I come to do your will
Your bodies are members of Christ
Come and see; we have found the Messiah
2027-01-17.alt: Year B. The memorial of St Antony, abbot, is not kept this year because it falls on Sunday. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-01-17.verse: He said to them, “Come and see.” They came and saw where he was staying, and they remained with him that day. It was about four o'clock in the afternoon.
theo: After the Epiphany and the Baptism, the first Sundays of Ordinary Time show how people come to Jesus. John the Baptist sees Jesus walk by and says, “Look, here is the Lamb of God!” Two of his disciples follow. Jesus turns and asks the first question he speaks in John's Gospel: “What are you looking for?” They answer with another question: “Rabbi… where are you staying?” And he says: “Come and see.” They stay with him that day; John even remembers the hour, “about four o'clock in the afternoon”. An encounter with Jesus is never forgotten.

Andrew immediately finds his brother Simon: “We have found the Messiah.” He brings him to Jesus, who looks at him and gives him a new name: “You are to be called Cephas”, Peter, rock. Faith spreads from person to person, brother to brother. The first reading shows the boy Samuel learning to recognise God's call, thanks to old Eli: “Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening.” Every vocation needs someone who helps us hear.

St Paul reminds the Corinthians that this following involves the whole person: “your bodies are members of Christ… your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit… glorify God in your body.” Discipleship is not only ideas; it is where we go, what we do with our bodies, whom we stay with. The Psalm puts the answer on our lips: “Here I am… I delight to do your will.”
conn: John the Baptist's title for Jesus recalls the Passover lamb (Exodus 12) and the Servant led like a lamb (Isaiah 53:7). The priest repeats it before Communion.
Jesus' first words in John are a question: “What are you looking for?” (1:38). His first words to Mary Magdalene after the Resurrection are similar: “Whom are you looking for?” (20:15).
Literally “the tenth hour”. The precise detail suggests the memory of an eyewitness, perhaps the unnamed second disciple, traditionally John.
Andrew appears three times in John, always bringing someone to Jesus: Peter, the boy with the loaves (6:8–9), and the Greeks (12:20–22). He is the patron of missionaries.
The Aramaic kepha means rock; Greek Petros. A new name means a new mission, as with Abraham and Israel.
Samuel had not yet experienced the LORD; Eli, though weak as a father, recognised God's call and taught the boy to answer. God works even through imperfect guides.
altar: Before Communion the priest says the Baptist's words: “Behold the Lamb of God.” Like the first disciples, we come and see, and stay with him.
Our bodies are members of Christ. In Communion his Body joins ours, and we leave to glorify God in our bodies.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

family.explain: Two friends of John the Baptist followed Jesus. Jesus asked: what are you looking for? He said: come and see! They stayed with him all afternoon. Then Andrew ran to bring his brother Peter.
family.intention: We pray for young people, that they may hear God's call.
family.ask: Ask: “Who brought you to know Jesus? Whom can we bring?”

illus: A young man from Thrissur working in Dubai had stopped going to church. A colleague simply said one Friday: come with me to Mass; just come and see. He went, stayed for the coffee afterwards, and kept coming. Five years later he leads the parish youth group. He says: nobody argued with me; someone just invited me.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you asked your first disciples: what are you looking for? Here we are, looking for you. Let us come and see, and stay with you. Amen.
share: “Speak, for your servant is listening” (1 Samuel 3:10). How do I listen for God's voice?
“What are you looking for?” (John 1:38). What do I really seek?
“We have found the Messiah” (John 1:41). Whom can I bring to Jesus?

interc: For the Church, that she may be a home where people come and see Jesus.
For vocations to the priesthood and religious life.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the Gospel today shows us how the first disciples came to Jesus. John the Baptist sees Jesus walking by and says: look, here is the Lamb of God! Two of his disciples hear and follow Jesus.

Jesus turns and asks them: what are you looking for? (John 1:38). These are his first words in John's Gospel, and he asks each of us the same question. What are you really looking for? Money, success, love, peace? Behind all our desires is a longing for God.

They answer: Rabbi, where are you staying? And Jesus says: come and see. They went and stayed with him that day. It was about four o'clock in the afternoon (John 1:39). Decades later John still remembered the hour. A real encounter with Jesus changes a life.

Then Andrew finds his brother Simon and says: we have found the Messiah. He brings him to Jesus, who looks at him and gives him a new name, Peter, the rock (John 1:41–42). Faith spreads from person to person.

In the first reading the boy Samuel hears his name called three times and does not understand. Old Eli helps him: say, speak, LORD, for your servant is listening (1 Samuel 3:9). We all need an Eli to help us hear God, and we can be an Eli for someone else.

St Paul reminds us that our bodies are members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit. Following Jesus involves the whole of us. This week let us answer Jesus' question honestly, spend time staying with him, and invite one person to come and see. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus asked two friends: what are you looking for? Then he said: come and see! They stayed with him all afternoon and became his friends.
